Europe’s Defense Dilemma
summary: Fix and Fiott argue that Europe has three options to prepare for a future of limited or conditional U.S. support: It can hope for a more European NATO, develop an EU-based defense union, or create a more flexible European defense coalition of the willing to deter against Russia and absorb future shocks to the transatlantic relationship.

ai.sum: CFR analysis outlines three options for Europe to deter Russia amid limited or conditional US support: a more European NATO, an EU defense union, or a flexible coalition of the willing.

brief.summary: The authors argue that with U.S. support to Europe shrinking, Russia will remain Europe's main threat, and Europe needs to prepare for limited or conditional American protection. They lay out three models: a more European NATO, in which Europeans take primary responsibility for conventional defence while keeping U.S. nuclear backing; a European defence union built on the EU's mutual-defence and solidarity clauses (TEU Article 42(7) and TFEU Article 222); and a flexible coalition of willing European states, including Ukraine. They judge each model's military, political, legal and industrial costs, and conclude that a combination is the likeliest outcome. The authors say a European NATO offers the most continuity, the EU route suits a deeper U.S. withdrawal, and the coalition gives the most crisis flexibility but needs permanent NATO or EU support structures.
brief.argument: Europe should treat a more European NATO, an EU defence union and a willing-states coalition as complementary tracks, since no single model fully covers a future of limited U.S. protection.
recommendations: Focus on defence investment, capability development and expansion of the defence industry regardless of which model prevails.
Build a durable coalition of willing European states, including Ukraine, to supply political flexibility in a crisis.
Make the coalition complementary to permanent NATO or EU support structures rather than a substitute for them.
Develop the operational response architecture behind Article 42(7) so the mutual-defence clause becomes credible.
brief.turkey: The piece's assessment of a more European NATO, a coalition of willing states and a European defence industry bears on Türkiye's defence-industrial and alliance positioning as Europe rebalances its security architecture.

summary: Humanoid robots: the industry set to reshape our lives newspress_en Mon, 11/02/2026 - 04:25 Science & Technology To many, artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics are the defining new technologies of the early 21st century, and now the former is helping to design the latter. It is a brave new world. Robots are already deployed at scale in factories around the world, but the introduction of humanoid robots in a residential setting has only just begun, with recent advances…

ai.sum: An article surveys the humanoid robotics industry and its expected impact on society.

brief.summary: The authors argue that humanoid robots are moving from controlled settings such as factories and warehouses toward shops and homes, where unstructured conditions are the main obstacle. They describe two development tracks, physical manipulation and understanding requests, and note that combining them widens the range of work robots can do. Evidence includes BMW and GXO deployments, a Figure home trial in which task success rose from 9% to 56% after new training, and AgiBot's retail rollout. The piece also points to AI models such as Google DeepMind's Gemini Robotics as a way to transfer skills across robot designs. On commercial scale, IDC figures show shipments near 25,000 in the first half of 2026, with Chinese firms accounting for over 95%, helped by a dense supply base and state support. Prices are expected to fall, widening uptake.
brief.argument: Humanoid robots are beginning to leave structured industrial settings for homes and shops, and China's supply-chain and state backing is positioning it to dominate the market.

The exhibition, Between Endless Chants and Star Divination , continued the artist’s exploration of the bird in flight, through whose watchful eye he has captured Yemen's emotional and geographical landscapes. For more than a year, Al-Aqel has devoted himself to a new…

ai.sum: Yemeni artist Hakim Al-Aqel presented two painting collections at Villa Azad in Cairo.

brief.summary: The authors, writing in Al Majalla about an exhibition in Cairo, describe Yemeni artist Hakim Al-Aqel's new series, Between Endless Chants and Star Divination, which uses the perspective of a bird in flight to survey Yemen's landscapes and daily life. They argue that the work draws on Yemeni memory, heritage, rituals and ancient Sabaean symbolism, and that it depicts a country scarred by war and economic crisis yet still rich in colour and vitality. The piece traces how his technique has developed over a decade, from simple aerial viewpoints to layered compositions where the bird itself becomes visible to the people below. Music, landscape and his childhood in Taiz are presented as central to his imagination. The article is an arts review and carries no security or policy argument.
brief.argument: The authors argue that Al-Aqel's aerial paintings use a bird's-eye viewpoint to portray a rich, enduring Yemeni homeland and cultural memory despite war.

summary: Israel's elections and the limits of political change newspress_en Mon, 11/02/2026 - 03:44 Opinion Israelis voted on 27 October 2026 with their country at war on three fronts and their prime minister fighting for his political life. The result showed a nation that has lost faith in Benjamin Netanyahu but not in the doctrine he embodies. The numbers tell only part of the story. Netanyahu's bloc won 53 seats; the opposition led by Gadi Eisenkot, the former chief of staff, won…

ai.sum: Opinion piece argues Israel's elections show voter loss of faith in Netanyahu without rejection of his doctrine.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Israel's 27 October 2026 election, held during war on three fronts, shows a public that has lost faith in Netanyahu personally but not in the security doctrine he embodies. Netanyahu's bloc won 53 seats against 48 for Gadi Eisenkot's opposition, so coalition bargaining looms. They contend the campaign was a contest over how the state is managed rather than between peace and war camps, since Eisenkot differs from Netanyahu on execution, not doctrine. The doctrine they describe, expanding operations beyond borders to neutralise threats early and holding buffer zones, is presented as the security establishment's consensus that would outlast Netanyahu. Record turnout of 77.7% is read as a sign of deep polarisation, and Netanyahu is portrayed as retaining his base and remaining unignorable even in defeat.
brief.argument: Netanyahu's possible political fall would not bring a strategic shift, because the security doctrine since October 7 is a broad establishment consensus that the election did not challenge.

brief.summary: The article argues that the Republican Party faces likely losses in the 3 November 2026 US midterm elections, following the historical pattern in which the president's party usually loses congressional seats midway through a term. It notes rare exceptions, such as 1998 and 2002, when strong economic conditions or post-9/11 support helped the incumbent party. Polling, including a Reuters/Ipsos survey showing 47% Democratic versus 35% Republican intent, and Cook Political Report projections suggest Democrats could win a House majority, though US district-level polling is imprecise. The Senate is a tougher target for Democrats, who would need a net gain of four seats for a majority, and even three gains would leave Republicans in control via Vice President Vance's casting vote. The authors stress that holding only the House would allow blocking legislation and oversight but not full control of the agenda or veto over appointments.
brief.argument: Republicans are likely to lose the House in the 2026 midterms, but Democrats face a steeper path to control the Senate, so partial divided government is the most probable outcome.

She argues that the tech industry's earlier withdrawal from defence work was driven more by money than by ideology. The episode is framed as an exploration of how commercial technology shapes the future of warfare rather than a set of formal policy prescriptions.

title: Bibi and the Blockchain: When a Prime Minister Plans for Sanctions Evasion
summary: Benjamin Netanyahu’s interest in cryptocurrency reveals both the continuing power of financial sanctions and the current limits of technological attempts to circumvent them.

ai.sum: RUSI analysis examines Netanyahu's interest in cryptocurrency as a means of sanctions evasion.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Benjamin Netanyahu's reported plan to build a crypto-based 'bypass economy' against possible sanctions misreads what sanctions do. Drawing on Russia's experience, they hold that crypto and stablecoins can move money for specific transactions and support circumvention networks, but cannot replicate the wider benefits of access to the international financial system, such as correspondent banking, trade finance, insurance and investment. They identify liquidity limits, stablecoin risk and the need for counterparties to rewire payments as obstacles at national scale. They also stress that financial sovereignty depends on other actors' willingness to trust and accept the system, and that circumvention is not substitution. The piece concludes that governments seeking protection from isolation should focus on preventing sanctions rather than building alternative payment rails.
brief.argument: Crypto can move money for specific transactions but cannot substitute for the broader access to the international financial system that a sanctioned economy needs.
recommendations: Focus on preventing sanctions and their negative impact on the economy rather than building alternative payment systems.
Recognise that crypto offers payment transfer but not guaranteed counterparties, credit, insurance or investment.
Treat sanctions evasion as requiring a range of tools rather than a single crypto solution.
brief.turkey: The piece offers a cautionary comparison for Türkiye on how sanctions risk and alternative payment channels (as in Russia's case) affect economic resilience, though it does not address Türkiye directly.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Republicans face a serious risk of losing control of the US House of Representatives in the 3 November midterms, continuing a historical pattern in which the president's party loses seats midway through a term. They note that the rare exceptions, such as 1998 and 2002, came under special economic or post-9/11 conditions. They attribute mid-term losses to public dissatisfaction, lower turnout among ruling-party supporters, and higher turnout among opponents, and say Trump's appeals to his base reflect that worry. Citing a Reuters/Ipsos poll and Cook Political Report projections, they say Democrats could gain enough seats for a House majority, though district-level polling is imprecise. They judge the Senate a harder target for Democrats, who would need a net gain of four seats for a majority, and conclude that House control alone would allow oversight and blocking of legislation without full control of the agenda.
brief.argument: Republicans are likely to lose House control in the 2026 midterms, but winning the Senate is a much harder task for Democrats.

title: Europa braucht Antworten auf Russlands Sabotagekampagne

ai.sum: SWP calls for European answers to Russia's sabotage campaign.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Russia's sabotage campaign against Germany and Europe has multiplied since 2023-2024 and peaked this summer. Attacks on armaments plants, logistics hubs, critical infrastructure and drone overflights of military sites are carried out largely decentrally, using disposable and long-term agents. The piece reads these acts as serving several overlapping goals: probing gaps between national and Nato responsibilities, demonstrating Russian capability to unsettle populations, and eroding support for Ukraine. Existing German, EU and Nato responses are judged insufficient because classic deterrence works poorly below the threshold of armed conflict. The author attributes part of this grey zone to Western restraint, and calls for clearly defined red lines and consequences, naming the campaign as orchestrated while keeping public debate alert without treating every drone sighting as sabotage.
brief.argument: Russia's sabotage campaign exploits a grey zone below the threshold of armed conflict, and Western hesitation to set clear limits and consequences sustains it.
recommendations: Name the sabotage acts publicly as one orchestrated campaign with cumulative consequences for European states.
Define clear red lines and concrete consequences for sabotage below the threshold of armed conflict.
Close gaps at the seams between internal and external security responsibilities, including counter-drone defence.
Raise public awareness so that society can cope with the threat without treating every incident as sabotage.

brief.summary: The authors, in this CFR book announcement by Liana Fix, argue that Germany's shift from 'civilian power' to a leading European military power is a prism for the broader changes in Europe and the transatlantic alliance. Fix contends that the 'myth of pacifism' long shaped German identity even though Germany used military tools pragmatically, and that the 2022 Zeitenwende was delayed until doubts over US protection under Trump forced urgent planning. She outlines six possible pathways for a rearmed Germany, from a European defence alliance filling the US gap to nationalist or disintegrating outcomes. Three factors will decide the path: the future US role, European defence cooperation, and whether the far-right AfD can be contained. Fix also frames Germany's reckoning as a warning that no order can last without the power to defend it.
brief.argument: Germany's rearmament is a defining test of Europe's security, and its direction will depend on the US role, European cooperation, and the containment of the far right.

title: How to prevent an energy quarantine of Taiwan
summary: An all-of-the-above energy strategy in Taiwan can help the United States and allies deter a Chinese energy quarantine of the island. The post How to prevent an energy quarantine of Taiwan appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: An Atlantic Council analysis argues that Taiwan's energy strategy could help deter a Chinese energy quarantine of the island.

brief.summary: The authors argue Beijing is laying groundwork for an energy quarantine of Taiwan, using legal-enforcement framing to avoid calling it war. They contend China's energy self-sufficiency is rising through vehicle electrification, domestic output, overland Russian pipelines and large stockpiles, so the old US counter-blockade strategy is outdated. They assess Taiwan's exposure as high because its energy is almost wholly imported, and that the risk could peak in 2028-2029 due to economic divergence, Taiwan's January 2028 election, thin electricity reserve margins, US military strain and AI timelines. Their proposed deterrent is an all-of-the-above energy strategy, with priority on diesel generation and storage for northern Taiwan, where the capital depends on southern power transmission.
brief.argument: China is closing its energy vulnerability while Taiwan's exposure is acute, so the coalition should urgently build diesel-based energy resilience for Taiwan, especially in the north, before a quarantine risk peaks around 2028-2029.
recommendations: Pursue an all-of-the-above energy strategy for Taiwan, including expanded nuclear capacity and restarting the Maanshan plant by 2028
Adopt a 'north diesel, south renewables' generation approach and resource it effectively
Build a distributed diesel generation supply chain for northern Taiwan, spanning refinery output, storage and generators
Expand Taiwan's LNG and gas storage ties with the US and allies

summary: The next secretary-general of the United Nations will need to lead at a time of crises in all three pillars of the institution: peace and security, development, and human rights. In CFR’s UN Secretary-General Candidates Series, Rebeca Grynspan explains why she is suited for this moment.

ai.sum: CFR interview series features Rebeca Grynspan on how she would lead the United Nations as secretary-general.

brief.summary: The authors, Esther Brimmer and Alexander Sarchet of CFR, report on an on-the-record conversation with UN Secretary-General candidate Rebeca Grynspan, who heads UNCTAD. They argue the next secretary-general must lead through crises in peace and security, development and human rights. According to the piece, Grynspan believes the secretary-general should be an active negotiator, citing her Black Sea Grain Initiative experience and calling the UN risk-averse. She holds that development aid should aim at countries no longer needing it, with UN agencies providing capacity-building, and that the UN should be demand-driven. She presents herself as an insider able to reform the system. The authors conclude the selection remains unpredictable, since no candidate yet has all five permanent members' assent.
brief.argument: Grynspan's insider experience and active-negotiator approach make her a strong candidate to lead UN reform amid crises across all three pillars.

UN should focus on the functions where it is uniquely placed and do more with less
UN development support should be demand-driven, shaped by countries' own priorities

title: Europe’s China Auto Deal
summary: Europe’s auto deal with China is a good start. But containing China’s export boom will require a much broader response.

ai.sum: Commentary on Europe's auto deal with China and the need for a broader response to China's export boom.

brief.summary: The author argues that the new EU-China auto deal is a useful first step, but that it only stops the bleeding. Chinese auto exports are surging because China's domestic market is shrinking while its factories sit mostly idle, so exporting is the only way for many firms to stay profitable. The deal caps Chinese hybrid imports, sets tiered tariffs on battery electric cars and a 10 percent tariff on combustion cars, but leaves parts and battery imports untouched and imposes no inward-investment conditions on Chinese transplant factories. The author says Europe must extend the approach to chemicals, machinery and other sectors and build a broader instrument, such as a European Section 301-style tool, while noting that China's currency and industrial policy will ultimately decide how far managed trade must expand.
brief.argument: The EU-China auto deal is a good start, but containing China's export surge will require a much broader European trade and industrial response.
recommendations: Extend negotiated tariff-rate quotas and safeguards beyond autos to chemicals, machinery and other sectors where Chinese imports are surging.
Develop a broad, targeted tariff-based instrument, similar to a European Section 301, as a credible fallback if negotiations fail.
Adopt industrial policy tools, such as those in the proposed Industrial Accelerator Act, to require Chinese investors to localise more than final assembly in Europe.
Pursue a coherent European policy on inward investment, including joint-venture or technology-transfer conditions.

title: Global Monetary Policy Tracker
summary: CFR’s Global Monetary Policy Tracker compiles data from 54 countries around the world to highlight significant global trends in monetary policy. Who is tightening policy? Who is loosening policy? And what is the policy stance of the world as a whole?

ai.sum: CFR publishes a tracker of monetary policy stances across 54 countries.

brief.summary: The authors present an interactive tracker covering 54 large countries, mostly inflation-targeting, that shows which central banks are tightening (red) or loosening (green) monetary policy and by how much, measured from the most recent policy trough or peak. Each country's growth, inflation, policy rate and date of last rate move can be inspected, and quantitative easing is flagged. A global summary index runs from -10 (all easing) to +10 (all tightening), weighting each country's stance by its currency's share of global foreign exchange reserves, so the US dollar carries about 62 percent weight. A country counts as tightening or easing if it has moved rates in the past three months or is expected to within three months, and QE counts as easing. The tracker lets users change the month and year to see how policy has shifted, and filter by policy-rate level. It is a monitoring tool rather than an argument, and it links to the CFR's other global trackers.
brief.argument: A reserve-weighted index of central bank rate moves across 54 countries can show, over time, whether the world as a whole is tightening or easing monetary policy.

brief.summary: This digest, by War on the Rocks, gathers Ukrainian commentary to show how Ukrainians debate war, politics and public life beyond the battlefield. The featured item is a Radio NV interview with Yurii Butusov, a drone company commander, who describes Operation Veles near Kupiansk as the world's first underground offensive, in which Ukrainian troops advanced 15 kilometers through a fortified gas pipeline. He welcomes a reported order barring corrupt officials from military posts, though he argues it could have been issued without one. He criticises the government's review of mobilization exemptions as a populist, Soviet-style campaign that breeds corruption. Instead he calls for confidential, sector-based workforce planning that inventories military and civilian manpower before deciding who can be recruited. The rest of the text is largely members-only, so the wider argument on corruption and transparency is not visible.
brief.argument: Ukraine's mobilization reform should rest on confidential, sector-based workforce planning rather than populist, announcement-driven exemption reviews that encourage corruption.
recommendations: Inventory available human resources in both the military and civilian sectors before changing recruitment rules
Determine recruitable civilians by order, age and fitness, and identify those in critical infrastructure or the defence industry
Conduct workforce planning confidentially rather than through one-off public initiatives

ai.sum: Hudson Institute commentary argues that service members voting strengthens the American republic.

brief.summary: The author, a former Army lieutenant, argues that service members voting strengthens the republic and that military participation in elections should be encouraged. He notes that over 300,000 troops were unregistered in 2024 and only about 67% of active-duty personnel were registered, with fewer than half voting, largely because of training schedules and competing priorities. He defends Defense Secretary Hegseth's one-day stand-down for voter registration against critics who called it partisan, and contrasts it with the previous administration's extremism stand-down, which he says treated troops as suspects. Drawing on Civil War and World War II precedents and the Founders' concern about a detached standing army, he contends that citizen-soldiers should vote while remaining non-partisan in their official conduct.
brief.argument: Encouraging service members to register and vote is a non-partisan duty that keeps the military connected to the republic it defends.
recommendations: Hold a dedicated voter registration and absentee ballot stand-down in every election year.
Keep voting assistance officers in every unit and installation.
Maintain the rule that bars active-duty troops from partisan campaigning while encouraging their civic participation.

title: Putin is “Ready for War”: Is Europe Ready?

Tsiporah Fried Visiting Senior Fellow Tsiporah Fried Commentary Caption Finland’s President Alexander Stubb addresses journalists following a telephone call between himself and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Helsinki, Finland, on October 27, 2026. (Getty Images) Toggle Table of Contents Contents Contents…

ai.sum: A commentary argues Putin is ready for war and asks whether Europe is prepared, citing Finnish President Stubb's call with Putin.

brief.summary: The authors, through an interview with Tsiporah Fried of the Hudson Institute, argue that Vladimir Putin's claim that Russia is ready for war with Europe, paired with insistence that it does not want one, is a coercive strategy meant to seize control of the escalation and de-escalation debate and portray Europe's rearmament as the provocation. They contend the 'hybrid warfare' framing is outdated: Russia treats hybrid, conventional and nuclear tools as one continuum, so Europe should think in terms of strategic confrontation. On Europe's readiness, they identify vulnerabilities in mass and endurance, slow industrial timelines ("It's a question of speed"), dependence on US capabilities, and weak civil-military resilience, urging a 'total defence' approach. They judge deterrence increasingly a contest of conventional credibility and American commitment, and see Europe's divisions over dialogue with Moscow as exploitable by Putin.
brief.argument: Putin's 'ready for war' message is a coercive move to control escalation, and Europe's response must shift from hybrid-warfare thinking to strategic confrontation, closing industrial, military and societal gaps while keeping US commitment in place.
recommendations: Shorten industrial and procurement timelines so production can sustain a prolonged conflict.
Build total defence, linking military, civil authorities and private firms to protect infrastructure and supply chains.
Impose proportionate, collective costs in response to Russian provocations, such as attacks on Black Sea shipping, to restore deterrence credibility.
Keep the US military presence and integrated command structure in Europe while Europeans take on more conventional defence.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Washington should replace the C5+1 format with a C6+1 that includes Azerbaijan, which the five Central Asian states have already brought into their own consultative leaders' format (the C6). They make three points: Central Asia's landlocked position surrounded by Russia, China, Afghanistan and Iran makes the Caspian and Azerbaijan the most viable westward route, as shown by past U.S. reliance on Azerbaijan during the Afghan war and the growing importance of the Middle Corridor; Azerbaijan already has deep cultural, economic and diplomatic ties with the region, including through the Organization of Turkic States; and the C6 is already meeting and setting shared priorities. They add that expanding the format could support the Trump administration's Azerbaijan-Armenia peace efforts and connectivity. They present the change as an easy diplomatic step.
brief.argument: Washington should expand the C5+1 to a C6+1 by including Azerbaijan, reflecting both regional geography and the format the Central Asian states themselves have chosen.
recommendations: Include Azerbaijan in the C5+1 format at the next ministerial, making it a C6+1.
Treat Azerbaijan's participation as central to U.S. access to Central Asia via the Caspian and Middle Corridor.
Use the format change to support Azerbaijan-Armenia normalization and regional connectivity.
brief.turkey: The proposal implies a more prominent Azerbaijani role in U.S.-led Central Asia engagement, which would sit alongside Türkiye's own Turkic-world and Middle Corridor interests, though the piece does not address Türkiye directly.

ai.sum: Arab News commentary assesses the first budget of Chancellor Burnham amid difficult economic conditions in the UK.

brief.summary: The authors examine Prime Minister Andy Burnham's first budget, delivered by Chancellor John Healey, against a backdrop of economic discontent and security threats from Russia, Iran and East Asia. They argue the budget was a mixed bag for defence: it closed a £4.7 billion gap in the Defence Investment Plan and pledged 3 percent of GDP on defence by 2030, but offered no credible path to that target until next year's spending review. They warn that projected nominal cuts by 2028 would mean a real-terms reduction, which looks poor as Europe is expected to spend more. Drawing a parallel with Neville Chamberlain's 1937 budget, they note that even a leader remembered for appeasement prioritised rearmament. They conclude that the lack of clarity will worry allies in Washington and Europe and may signal weakness to adversaries.
brief.argument: Healey's budget filled the immediate defence funding gap and pledged 3 percent of GDP by 2030, but without a credible, detailed path to that target the spending plans leave Britain looking weak to allies and adversaries alike.
recommendations: Set out a concrete, credible path to 3 percent of GDP on defence before the next spending review.
Avoid nominal and real-terms defence spending falls by 2028.
Give allies in Washington and Europe clarity on how NATO spending targets will be met.

title: Scowcroft Strategy Scorecard: Grading Canada’s second-ever national security strategy
summary: For only the second time in its history, Canada has a new national security strategy. Does it match the clarity with which Prime Minister Mark Carney has described the challenges the country faces? Atlantic Council experts weigh in. The post Scowcroft Strategy Scorecard: Grading Canada’s second-ever national security strategy appeared first on Atlantic Council .

ai.sum: Atlantic Council assesses Canada's second national security strategy, released under Prime Minister Mark Carney.

brief.summary: The Atlantic Council's Scowcroft Center scores Canada's new national security strategy, The Plan for a Stronger Canada, only the second of its kind. The authors broadly praise its distinctiveness and clear focus on sovereignty and economic security, which they read as a response to strained relations with the United States and to Carney's Davos framing of a rupture in the global order. Their main criticism is thin strategic context: the strategy barely names adversaries, Russia and China are absent, and the United States is referenced only obliquely. They also find the implementation details sparse, with the real substance deferred to five forthcoming sub-strategies. Several authors question whether the economic-sovereignty approach can compensate for reduced integration with Washington, and note that the four-year review cycle is a welcome feature.
brief.argument: The authors argue that Canada's strategy gives clear sovereignty-focused goals and lines of effort, but it falls short because it does not name threats and offers too little implementation detail.
recommendations: Explicitly identify Canada's adversaries and threats so the public shares a cohesive threat perception.
Provide concrete implementation details and delivery timelines before relying on the forthcoming sub-strategies.
Explain why the listed strategic capability sectors matter and how each links to the threats Canada faces.
Clarify how the sovereignty and economic-security goals will be resourced and reconcile deeper international partnerships with reduced integration with the United States.
